cards.text: Friend, this one's heavy, so pull up a stool. Babylon's army has burned Jerusalem and broken down her walls (Jeremiah 52:13-14). Now a poet looks at the city and cries, "How lonely lies the city, once so full of people!"

cards.question: Everything has flipped. She was great among the nations, and now she's a widow. And the princess of the provinces? She has become a ___.

cards.text: Night falls, and she weeps aloud with tears upon her cheeks. She's got a long list of lovers and friends, so let's see who comes knocking.

cards.question: The poet says all of Jerusalem's friends have betrayed her. What have those friends become?
Out of all her lovers, at least one comes to comfort Jerusalem.

cards.text: Judah has gone into exile, under affliction and harsh slavery. All her pursuers have caught up with her in the middle of her distress.

cards.question: Judah is in exile now, living among the nations. What does she find there?

cards.text: Even the roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to her appointed feasts. Her gates are deserted, her priests groan and her maidens grieve.

cards.question: Jerusalem's foes have become her masters. The poet says the LORD has brought her this grief. Because of what?

cards.text: Her children have gone away as captives before the enemy. All the splendor has departed from the Daughter of Zion.

cards.question: The poet says Jerusalem's princes are like deer that find no pasture. What happens when the hunter comes?

cards.text: In her wandering, Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old. I did that in the junk drawer, friend, except my good old days were a COUNTER.

cards.question: When Jerusalem's people fell into enemy hands, no help came. The poet says her enemies looked away in shame.

cards.text: The poet doesn't soften it: Jerusalem has sinned greatly. Everyone who honored her now despises her, and she groans and turns away.

cards.question: Her uncleanness stains her skirts. The poet says Jerusalem saw her downfall coming a long way off.
There's no one to comfort her. Then Jerusalem herself cries out for the first time. Who does she ask to look on her affliction?

cards.text: The adversary seizes all her treasures. And she has seen the nations walk into her sanctuary.

cards.question: The nations entered Jerusalem's sanctuary. They were the very ones God had ___ to enter His assembly.

cards.text: All her people groan as they search for bread. Then Jerusalem cries out again: "Look, O LORD, and consider, for I have become despised."

cards.question: To keep themselves alive, Jerusalem's people trade their treasures for food.

cards.text: Up to now the poet's been doing most of the talking. Now Jerusalem grabs the mic and calls out to everyone on the road: "Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by?"

cards.question: Jerusalem tells everyone passing by to look around and see. What does she want to know?

answers.text: If any sorrow is like hers

cards.question: Jerusalem says the LORD made her suffer on the day of His fierce anger.

cards.text: She doesn't just say it hurts, friend. She paints it: the Lord sent fire from on high that overpowered her bones, and He spread a net for her feet.

cards.question: The net the Lord spreads for Jerusalem's feet carries her safely home.

cards.text: Then her sins get a picture of their own: they're bound into a yoke, knit together by His hand. And friend, I thought years under paper and dust were heavy.

cards.question: Jerusalem says her transgressions are bound into a yoke and draped over her ___.

cards.text: Friend, this is where I'd put the dough down for a minute. The Lord has broken her strength, handed her over to those she cannot withstand and rejected all the mighty men in her midst.

cards.question: Jerusalem says the Lord summoned an army against her, and like grapes in a winepress, He has trampled the Virgin Daughter of Judah. What is that picture saying?

cards.text: She weeps, and her children are destitute because the enemy has prevailed. Then the poet steps back in, and friend, Zion stretches out her hands with no one to comfort her.

cards.question: The poet calls God's people Jacob, after their forefather Jacob, Isaac's son. What does he say the LORD has decreed against Jacob?
Jerusalem speaks again. She says the LORD is ___, yet she rebelled against His command.

cards.text: Now she's calling out to everyone in earshot: listen, and look upon her suffering. Her young men and maidens have gone into captivity, and she called out to her lovers too.

cards.question: When Jerusalem called out to her lovers, they came running to help her.

cards.text: Her priests and elders died in the city while they searched for food to keep themselves alive. Then she turns to the LORD, and friend, I can hear it in every word: "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!"

cards.question: Jerusalem says she is churning within and her heart is pounding. What reason does she give?

cards.text: Outside, the sword bereaves, and inside, there is death. People hear her groaning, and friend, there's that line again: no one to comfort her.

cards.question: Jerusalem's enemies hear about her trouble, and they are glad that the LORD caused it.
Jerusalem asks the LORD to bring the day He has announced and to deal with her enemies. How does she ask Him to deal with them?

answers.text: As He has dealt with her

cards.text: And the poem ends right where her heart is: "For my groans are many, and my heart is faint."

findings.problem: The right answer 'Her many transgressions' sounds more like the Bible than the plain wrong answers 'Her weak walls' and 'Her proud kings', so it stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The joke depends on the baker knowing Papa Dorin used to sit on the Millers' counter. Nothing earlier in the lesson sets that up, and onboarding only covers the drawer. Without that, 'my good old days were a COUNTER' reads as 'huh?'

rule.text: A callback only works if its setup came earlier in this lesson or conversation.

findings.problem: The story card has three things happening: the Lord breaks her strength, hands her over to those she cannot withstand (1:14), and rejects her mighty men (1:15).

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The story card has three things happening across two verses: Jerusalem calls on everyone to listen and look, her young men and maidens go into captivity (1:18), and she calls out to her lovers (1:19).

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The question states a Bible fact from outside the passage, that Jacob is the people's forefather and Isaac's son, without a reference (for example Genesis 25:26).

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.
